reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes a rapid-return crypto opportunity, advertising +320% and claiming that 0.3 BNB produced more than 10.7 BNB within minutes. It instructs viewers to connect or install a wallet, pay gas fees, deploy a contract, and supply liquidity, while suggesting that higher deposits can produce higher returns. Although it includes an educational disclaimer and loss warning, it directs viewers toward contract code and an external flash-loan tool while the claimed returns and destination behavior remain unverified.

opening.argument: Judge, the return claim should be read alongside the video's explicit limits. The speaker says returns differ with network volume and liquidity, including the possibility of only a small return [1]. The description warns that the method will not work on testnets [2], and the closing slide tells viewers to follow carefully to prevent losses and calls the material educational [3]. Those cautions do not prove the method works, but they weigh against reading the example as a promise that every viewer will receive the displayed gain.

citations.quote: the return is different every time depending on the network volume and the amount of liquidity you put in. Sometimes you will get a small amount
IMPORTANT NOTICE : This method does not work on testnets !

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening rightly notes the striking gain claim, but the speaker describes it as one example [1], then expressly says results vary and can be small [2]. Wallet connection, gas fees and liquidity are part of the procedure shown; their presence alone does not establish that the claimed result is guaranteed or that funds are diverted. The loss warning on the final slide matters when judging how the video presents that risk [3].

citations.quote: In this example I've done, you'll see how I used just 0.3 BNB to gain over 10.7 BNB in just minutes.
Sometimes you will get a small amount, while other times you can hit it big like we did here.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Variability and a loss warning do not neutralize the pitch. The video leads with a claim of turning 0.3 BNB into more than 10.7 BNB in minutes [1], says a higher deposit brings higher potential profit [2], and instructs viewers to supply liquidity and execute the contract [3]. The cautions do not verify the return or explain what the supplied contract does with a viewer's funds.

opening.argument: Judge, the video's structure is that of a technical walkthrough. It introduces a step-by-step tutorial [1], explains how to create and compile a Solidity file in Remix [2], and shows the compiler interface [3]. It also walks through adding a network to a browser wallet [4]. The reported return is part of the demonstration, but these concrete operational steps are central to what the viewer is shown. The record does not independently validate the result; equally, an unvalidated demonstration is not, by that fact alone, evidence that the creator is taking viewers' funds.

citations.quote: Step by Step Tutorial
name the file something like FlashLoan.sol Sol now you want to paste in the smart contract code into this new file.
the metamask wallet comes with the ethereum network so we need to add the binance smart chain network

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference opening identifies real instructions to connect a wallet, pay fees and place liquidity. Those steps also fit the tutorial's stated sequence of compiling and deploying a contract [1]. Its return figure is introduced as an example [2], not accompanied by a claim that every run pays the same amount; the speaker later says the return differs [3]. The opening does not establish from those steps alone what the contract ultimately does.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The technical walkthrough is precisely how viewers are moved toward the risky action. The speaker directs them to use contract code supplied with the video [1], says a higher initial deposit raises potential profit [2], and instructs them to send liquidity before executing the contract [3]. Calling that sequence educational does not resolve the unverified earnings claim or the risk of following supplied code with real funds.

opening.argument: Judge, the description presents an arbitrage-tool link [1], while the narrated payments are identified as contract-creation gas fees and liquidity for the viewer's newly created contract [2][3]. That evidence warrants caution about the tool and code, but it does not by itself identify a payment to the creator, a credential request, or a fixed payout obligation. The speaker even describes smaller returns as possible [4]. The stronger inference from the supplied record is promotion of a risky crypto workflow, not a demonstrated mechanism by which the promoter receives viewers' deposits.

liquidity to make your new token have a value you can actually trade against.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening points to an external tool, wallet interaction and a higher-deposit incentive, all fair reasons to scrutinize the video. But the cited fee is described as a gas fee for creating a contract [1], and the liquidity instruction concerns the newly created token [2]. Neither quote establishes who ultimately receives those funds. The video presents an example of a large gain, while also acknowledging that a run may return only a small amount [3].

citations.quote: Gas Fees to create your new token contract
liquidity to make your new token have a value you can actually trade against.
Sometimes you will get a small amount

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A scam mechanism need not include an explicit payment to the creator or a guaranteed payout. Here the speaker supplies code to copy [1], directs viewers to fund a contract [2], and tells them to execute it while presenting a rapid tenfold-plus gain [3]. The absence of a verified recipient does not make that funded-contract promotion ordinary commerce, particularly when the supplied evidence does not establish the code's behavior.
